text: Animal movement control (ការគ្រប់គ្រងការផ្លាស់ទីសត្វ) matters because an apparently healthy animal can carry infection before showing signs -- 'it looked healthy at the market' is not proof of disease-free status. Know the source of purchased animals where possible, avoid visibly sick animals, and keep simple purchase/sale/movement records. New animals should be kept separate and observed before joining the herd or flock, with the isolation period set by disease risk and veterinary guidance, never a fixed universal number. Animals returning from markets, other farms, communal grazing, or breeding services may have been exposed to infection and should be handled the same way as newly purchased animals. Livestock markets mix animals from many farms and are a real transmission risk regardless of whether any animal looks sick. Vehicles, cages, ropes, footwear, and equipment can carry pathogens between farms even without a sick animal present -- clean equipment that's contacted livestock from elsewhere before reusing it. During the wet season, muddy roads and wet equipment complicate hygiene; during the dry season, heat stress during transport and animal concentration around water sources add risk. CRITICAL RULE: sick animals should NEVER be taken to market to recover some value before they deteriorate -- if a serious contagious disease is suspected, stop unnecessary movement and sales entirely and get veterinary or official guidance first. This matters especially for FMD and ASF, where movement has consequences beyond the individual farm. Do not invent a breed, vaccination status, or local movement regulation the farmer hasn't provided.
